bham-01-tip.caption:
Confidence in business looks like a personality. Most of the time it is information.

The man who prices a kitchen in four minutes is not bolder than the one who says he will ring you back. He has done eleven of them and he knows what the last one cost him in materials, in labour and in the day he lost to it. The figure is in his head because it was written down somewhere first.

We see it across Birmingham every week. Two shops on the same parade with the same footfall. One can tell you on a Tuesday which lines are carrying the rest of the shop. The other finds out in October, from us, when the year is already spent.

The gap between them is not talent and it is not luck. It is a record kept well enough to ask questions of.

You do not need a system to begin. You need to know what came in, what went out and what it was for. Everything else is built on top of that, including the nerve to charge properly for your work.
bham-01-tip.ask: Worth keeping for a week when the nerve goes.
bham-01-tip.title: Confidence is mostly knowing your own numbers

bham-02-acq.caption:
Most people do not get caught out because they stopped caring. They get caught out because the number turned up bigger than they had pictured, in a month when the van had already broken down and the shop was three staff short.

That part is ours. We do your figures while there is still room to do something about them, so you hear the amount from us in good time, in plain words, with the reference you need to pay it. No letter to decode. No finding out in February what November could have told you.

Knowing the figure early changes what you can do with it. You can put a bit by each week instead of finding all of it at once. You can decide whether the new machine waits until after the year end. You can see what the quiet weeks after Christmas look like before you are standing in them.

We are a small local firm, and we would rather tell you something useful early than something true too late. If that is the way you would like it done, come and talk to us.
bham-02-acq.ask: Pass this to someone who dreads opening the post.
bham-02-acq.title: Know the figure early enough to do something about it

bham-03-acq.caption:
There is a difference between an accountant you email and an accountant you can stand in front of.

Ours is at 22-42 Washwood Heath Road, Saltley, B8 1RB, open Monday to Friday, 10:00 to 16:00. You can park, walk in, put the folder on the desk and point at the bit you do not understand. We will turn the screen round so you can see what we are doing with it.

That matters more than people expect. Some things are hard to explain in an email and easy to explain across a desk, so they get left, and left things grow. Asked out loud, the same question takes four minutes.

A takeaway, a barber's, a minicab firm, a groundworks outfit, a unit on an industrial estate, a shop on a parade. We know the trades round here because they are our neighbours. Come and see us, or message first and we will put the kettle on.
bham-03-acq.ask: Know somebody who has never met their accountant? Send it on.
bham-03-acq.title: An office on Washwood Heath Road you can walk into

bham-04-acq.caption:
Most questions about a business are small. Can I claim this. Do I need to register yet. Is this invoice right. None of them is worth a meeting and all of them are easy to put off, so they sit there for a month and get expensive.

So send them. WhatsApp is the quickest way to reach us and a person reads it, not a queue and not a bot. You get a straight answer in plain words, and you get it in writing, so when the same thing comes round in March you can scroll back and find it rather than ask again.

We would far rather answer twenty small questions in November than untangle one large one in January. The small ones cost us a few minutes. The large one costs you a decision you had to make in the dark.

If what you have is bigger than a message, the first half hour with us is free. Either way, start by asking.
bham-04-acq.ask: Keep this one so the number is to hand when you need it.
bham-04-acq.title: Send the small question, get a straight answer

bham-05-edu.caption:
If you are VAT-registered and you buy second-hand to sell on, there is a second way of working out the VAT, and it is worth knowing about.

Normally VAT is worked out on the full selling price. Under the margin scheme for second-hand goods, works of art, antiques and collectors' items, it is worked out on your margin instead, which is the difference between what you paid for the item and what you sold it for. The VAT due is one-sixth, or 16.67%, of that margin. One-sixth of the margin, not one-sixth of the price: that is the bit people get wrong.

It is optional and you apply it yourself. The price of it is record-keeping. You keep a stock book with a stock number in sequence for each item, the purchase date, the purchase invoice number, what you paid, who you bought it from and a description, and then the sale date, the sales invoice number, what you sold it for, who to, the margin and the VAT at one-sixth. Keep all of it for 6 years, and longer than that for anything still sitting in stock.

Where it does not reach: an item you were charged VAT on when you bought it can never go in, and nor can precious metals, investment gold or precious stones. Miss the scheme's conditions and you are back to VAT on the full selling price. Second-hand vehicles, caravans, houseboats, horses, part-exchange, auctioneers and unredeemed pawn all have separate rules of their own, so do not assume this page covers them.

If your stock is high volume and low value, there is a variant built for that. Ask us which one fits what you actually sell.
bham-05-edu.ask: Hold on to this before your next buying trip.
bham-05-edu.title: VAT on your margin, not on the full selling price

bham-06-edu.caption:
If you run a payroll, or you are a contractor taking deductions off subcontractors, the money you held back in the last tax month has a date on it.

Paying electronically, the date is the 22nd of the next tax month. For the tax month running 6 November to 5 December, that is 22 December 2026. For 6 December to 5 January, it is 22 January 2027. If you still post a cheque, it has to reach HMRC by the 19th instead.

The detail that catches good people out is what HMRC measures. Its own manual counts the payment as on time when it has cleared funds for the full amount by the 22nd, not when you pressed send. Faster Payments usually lands the same day or the next one. Bacs takes several working days, and December is short of them: 25 and 28 December 2026 and 1 January 2027 are bank holidays. Worth knowing too that 19 December 2026 falls on a Saturday, so a posted cheque realistically needs to be with HMRC by Friday 18 December.

Who this does not bind: employers whose average monthly payment is under £1,500, which is under £18,000 a year. They may pay quarterly instead, by the 22nd after the quarter ends, so the 6 October to 5 January quarter is due 22 January 2027. If you have no PAYE scheme at all, or you are the subcontractor having deductions taken off you rather than paying them over, none of this is yours.

When you pay, use your 13-character accounts office reference with the 4-digit period number on the end. Wrong period number is the commonest reason a payment sits in the wrong place.
bham-06-edu.ask: Saved somewhere handy, this gives you both the December and the January date.
bham-06-edu.title: The 22nd is the date, and cleared funds is the test

bham-07-edu.caption:
The day you take on your first employee, one insurance policy stops being optional.

Employers' liability cover has to be at least £5,000,000 for claims arising from any one occurrence, including the costs and expenses that come with them, and it has to be with an insurer authorised by the FCA. That figure is set in regulation 3 of the Employers' Liability (Compulsory Insurance) Regulations 1998, and it applies from the moment you become an employer, not from the end of your first month.

There are two penalties attached. £2,500 for each day you are not properly insured, and £1,000 for not having the certificate where your employees can get at it or for not producing it to an inspector who asks. Since 1 October 2008 you can satisfy the display duty electronically, as long as the people who work for you can reasonably get to it. The old duty to keep certificates for 40 years was removed on the same date, so there is no statutory retention period now, though keeping the old ones is still sensible because an illness claim can surface decades after the work.

Who it leaves out: an employer whose only employee is a close family member, meaning a spouse, civil partner, parent, child, grandparent, sibling, or a step or half relative. A single-director company where that director owns at least half the share capital, which sits inside the Schedule 2 exemptions in the 1998 Regulations and so often needs no policy at all. And a genuinely self-employed person with nobody on the books.

One more thing worth saying plainly: this is not public liability insurance and it is not your van insurance. Those are different policies doing different jobs. If you are about to put somebody on the books, get this one sorted first.
bham-07-edu.ask: Someone you know is about to take on staff. Send it to them.
bham-07-edu.title: Your first employee and the £5 million cover rule

bham-08-joke.caption:
Prices have a way of turning into furniture. You worked the list out once, you had it printed nicely, and now it is simply part of the wall.

Meanwhile the wholesaler has been up twice, the electric has been up, the lad you pay has had a rise because he earned one, and the thing that used to cost you four pounds does not cost you four pounds any more. Nothing on that sign knows about any of it.

The fix is not a dramatic increase. It is one quiet afternoon working out what a single thing you sell actually costs you to put in front of a customer today. The materials, the time it takes, and its share of the rent, the van and the insurance. Then read the sign again.

Usually the gap per line is small, and small per line across a whole year is the difference between a business that pays you properly and one you are quietly subsidising out of politeness.

And if you cannot work out what a job costs you, that is the thing to sort out first, before any price changes. Bring in your last three months and we will work it out with you.
bham-08-joke.ask: Forward this to whoever has not touched their price list since 2019.
bham-08-joke.title: The sign is still readable, so the prices stay

bham-09-joke.caption:
Every year the phone goes early on 30 January. Same tone of voice every time, somewhere between cheerful and sweating.

It is never a small question either. It is never "what box does this go in". It is "did I ever register", or "how much do I owe", or "is it this January or next January", asked in the one day of the year when nothing can be found out quickly.

The truth underneath the joke is dull. The work itself is not hard. Adding up a year of takings, matching it to a bank statement and finding what you spent on the business is a few hours of patient sorting. What makes it hard is that none of it can be laid hands on in a hurry.

So the thing worth changing is not really the month. It is where the year lives. One bank account the business actually uses, one folder for the invoices, one place on the phone for the photographs of receipts. Do that and "did I ever register" and "how much do I owe" become questions with answers sitting in them. Spread the same year across a van, a drawer and three phones and no amount of time will rescue it.

If you are reading this and you know it is you, do not start with the calendar. Start with being able to put your hand on the year. Ask us what to keep and where to keep it, and the phone call stops being that phone call.
bham-09-joke.ask: Send it to the one who always rings on the 30th.
bham-09-joke.title: The phone call that always comes on 30 January

bham-10-quote.caption:
Benjamin Franklin put this in Poor Richard's Almanack, and it has outlived almost everything else in there.

It is not really about being tight with money. It is about scale, and how badly people judge it. A business rarely sinks because of one terrible decision. It sinks because of eleven small ones that nobody added up: the subscription for the software you stopped using, the card machine on the old rate, the van insurance that renewed itself at a worse price, the £9 a month that has been going out since 2022 for a reason nobody can remember.

Individually, none of them is worth an evening. Together they are somebody's wages.

It is an hour of work that pays for itself, and an hour that is very easy to keep putting off. Open the bank statement. Read every outgoing, line by line, and ask what it is for. Cancel what you cannot answer for. Ring the ones you can and ask for a better rate, because quite often there is one and they are waiting to be asked.

Then put it in the diary for six months' time. Leaks do not announce themselves. You have to go looking.
bham-10-quote.ask: Tuck this away and give your outgoings an hour this week.
bham-10-quote.title: A small leak will sink a great ship
